utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is Wednesday, November 19th, 2008, and I welcome our witness. I also welcome the many representatives from the OTP, as well as their assistant. I welcome Mr. Seselj, and I also welcome Mr. Registrar, ushers, our court reporter and the interpreters in the booths helping us. We'll now continue with the cross-examination. Could the Registrar please tell me how much time is left. I believe it must be -- Mr. Seselj still has 30 minutes, unless I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, so far Mr. Seselj has used 49 minutes, which leaves him another 40 minutes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mrs. Bilic, did you live in Zagreb from 1991 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If not as a civil servant, as a native of Zagreb, perhaps, did you hear that in the area of the fairgrounds in Velesajam in Zagreb, there was a camp for detained civilians?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the existence of that camp was notified for the first time to the public by Dr. Zarko Puhovski, the professor of university and president of the Helsinki Council?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that, but from a few articles and press releases. I'm not familiar with any other information about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, if you are a ranking civil servant and have no information about the existence of a camp for detained Serb civilians, through which several thousand Serbs who lived in Zagreb had passed, then it doesn't surprise me that you're not aware of the other 220 camps for Serbs in Croatia. Here again, Mr. Dutertre is jumping to his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask Mr. Seselj to please give us documents when he is quoting figures. Otherwise, you know, he's speaking without any references, and we have absolutely no way to know whether what he's saying is true or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj. Yesterday, I told you, after the objection raised by the Prosecutor, that when you are submitting that you have such-and-such information, please also give us the source of this information. Tell us this is a report from such-and-such professor, published on such-and-such date at such-and-such place, country, and so on, just so we have an idea and so we know that what you are saying might be backed by at least some kind of document, because if need be, the Trial Chamber could refer to this document; and the Prosecutor could also refer to it if he has additional questions to ask. We're inviting you to do this. Of course, you're not legally bound to disclose all these documents to us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the existence of camps for Serb civilians from Zagreb in the area of the Zagreb Velesajam fairgrounds is a notorious fact, has been notorious for more than a decade. The witness says she's not aware of it. She may have read something in the newspapers, but she doesn't know anything about it. Her answer is perfectly satisfactory to me. It would be a problem for me if she said, "Yes, I know that camp existed. It was within the jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Interior or the Ministry of Justice. Our ministry was not involved, but that thing existed," because all Zagreb natives and locals know that it existed. And now, Mr. President, to answer definitively to the objection of Mr. Dutertre: If I were Prosecutor in this trial, I would have called Savo Strbac, the president of the NGO Veritas, yesterday. I have never met Savo Strbac in my life, but the Prosecution has been cooperating for years with Savo Strbac and his NGO, Veritas, and have received enormous quantities of material from them. If I were Prosecutor and if I had listened to the cross-examination yesterday, where the witness refers to information from NGO Veritas, I would have immediately contacted Veritas yesterday and asked, "Is this correct, is this true, is this accurate, can you give us the material?" Why can't Mr. Dutertre address Mr. Milorad Buha, president of the government of the Serbian Krajina in exile, because Milorad Buha is a member of the Serb Radical Party and he would have radically refused all contact with the OTP. So it doesn't surprise me that the Prosecution doesn't contact him. But you tied my ears, you blindfold me, you shut my mouth, you block visits from my advisers, communications with my associates, you block all dispatches by fax; and now you want me to provide documents. Why would I have to? I have reliable information. The Zagreb Velesajam fairgrounds was a camp through which several thousand Serbs civilians from Zagreb had passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to the latest allegations of Mr. Seselj on his communications, I would like to refer to what Mr. Mundis said yesterday extremely clearly regarding this issue. As to the rest, Mr. Seselj is mentioning Veritas; so if he wants to, it's up to him to bring documents and present documents in order to help the Trial Chamber decide in an informed fashion. If he wants to call this person for his Defence, he can do that. You know, it's not up to the Prosecution to do this in his place. That's just a few observations I wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Seselj, while you were talking, I was wondering maybe, you know, when you are asking for your -- were you're calling your witnesses, you might call this Savo Strbac, the director of this Veritas NGO. It doesn't necessarily have to be an exculpatory witness, it can also be a context witness, you know, somebody that is useful to help establish the truth. You can always call this witness if the Prosecutor decides it's not useful to call him on his side. But through your questions, you seem to indicate that there was a detainee camp for Serbs in Zagreb. The witness says she has no knowledge of this, so please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then later she said she may have read something in the newspapers, but nothing much. That was approximately her answer. Mr. President, it is not up to me to prove anything here. It is my job to ask questions. I have certain information, and I don't even have to tell you what my sources are. All I do is ask questions. My questions may be the most stupid questions in the world, but I have the right to them. I have that right, and I don't want to prove anything. Let the Prosecution prove whatever they want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you are entitled to put questions, that's true. That's a right that you have by the Statute. But I don't agree with you when you say that you're allowed to ask stupid questions or silly questions. That's not true, because then, you know, the issue is to provide you with counsel, because a counsel will not ask silly questions. If a counsel is asking stupid questions or silly questions, he's going to go against his code of ethics, and he might be penalized for that. You don't -- you cannot be penalized, but you must ask questions for your Defence. You're not here to waste our time. As such, I don't believe that your question was stupid, to know whether Serbs were detained in Zagreb or not. That is not fundamental regarding this expert's competence and expertise, but it might provide us with a general picture. However, she gave you her answer. Her answer is what it was. Now, you take note of the answer, and either you pursue the topic or you move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, just one sentence, Mr. President. If lawyers were really barred from asking stupid or idiotic questions, I assure you 80 per cent of advocates would have to leave the ICTY. I don't want to name names, but I will -- in fact, I could give you information about each one of them, and I could give you examples, specific examples from transcript. This threat that you will impose counsel on me doesn't bother me anymore. I'm completely indifferent to that. You can't impose counsel on me. You can try me in absentia, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I did not say that I was going to impose counsel on you. All I said was that when an accused is actually asking only silly questions, then the issue is that the solution might be to impose counsel on the accused. But here, we're in a different situation. I never said that when you were asking this question about Serbs being detained in Zagreb, that this question was stupid. I never said that. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. You have now assured me that I have not yet reached that degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, is it true a that your ministry, when it keeps records of missing persons, keeps a unified record of all missing persons who are citizens of Croatia, regardless of whether they disappeared?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. My ministry keeps a unified record of all missing citizens, that is, nationals of the Republic of Croatia, who went missing in relation to the war and whose families submitted a request for tracing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So what matters is for their families to submit a request?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This submission of a request for tracing by family is one of the basic criteria enabling a person to enter the category of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. So this list of yours, this list of missing persons, includes all Croat soldiers, regular Croatian soldiers, who as part of regular units of the Croatian Army were involved in the war in 1993 against Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and who were involved in 1995 in the war against Serbs especially in the Serbian Krajina, if they had gone missing in those war activities?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the obligation, and that's in the decree of the government of the Republic of Croatia, it's the obligation of the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons to search for all missing persons who went missing and who are citizens of Croatia, regardless of the location of their disappearance and the circumstances. According to that single criterion and that principle, the Commission for Missing Persons in Belgrade, which also has lists of missing persons, includes soldiers of the JNA who went missing in Croatia, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, or any other place. It is the obligation of the state to solve a case of its missing citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no objection regarding what is being said. However, I heard something in French that is not in the transcript, the fact that the research was done independently of the ethnic background. I heard that in French, and it didn't come in the English translation. Could we clarify this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please specify this, repeat exactly what you said regarding the ethnical background of the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons searches for all missing citizens, regardless of their origin, their nationality, their faith, and regardless of the side they were on at the time of their disappearance. Equally, the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons searches for missing citizens, nationals of the Republic of Croatia who went missing in the war, regardless of whether they disappeared in the Republic of Croatia or, for example, there were cases of missing persons who went missing in the territory of Serbia and in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, when Tudjman's regime was established, and that was sometime in May 1990, if my memory serves me well, shortly afterwards that regime enabled all Croats, regardless of where they were living, be it in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the US, or Canada, to obtain Croatian citizenship if they wished?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you have to know about this. Please don't tell me that you don't know even this. All Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina participated in the elections of Croatia, both presidential and parliamentary elections, and they have a special electoral unit in diaspora?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know there is an electoral unit for the diaspora, but I'm not aware that all Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina have the possibility to participate in parliamentary elections in the Republic of Croatia. But I know there is a special electoral unit for the diaspora.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How come I know about these things better than you do? And all these Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina who are citizens of the Republic of Croatia, and they are -- they were included in the books of citizens after the establishment of the Tudjman regime, if their family reports their disappearance, they automatically come onto your list?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that with the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons, we have records, and I may not be completely precise, of requests for tracing of about 60 persons who went missing in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you have a paper saying that?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with me, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't have it even in this paper, do you? And it's a very important piece of information, because I believe the number is higher than 60.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you give me a little time to try to find an overview of missing persons broken down by counties, which is part of the material I provided, I am sure that in that overview there is an indication of the number of persons who went missing outside the territory of Croatia. So we can establish the exact number. Therefore, this figure does exist in my -- in the additions to my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have time to give you that time. Tell me this: According to your official data, searches are still going on for about a thousand or 1.100 people?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I made my report, 1.076 persons were still being searched for. Those were persons about whom information was collected in the drive of 1994. 874 of them went missing in the Operation Storm, which makes --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let us look at it separately, because it's separate in your report. 874 -- how many Serbs did you say went missing in Operations Storm and Flash?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the military police Operations Flash and Storm, according to tracing requests submitted by the families of missing persons, thus according to the same criteria used by the ICRC, and the same criteria on the basis of which the lists of missing persons were compiled in 1991 and 1992, at this time we have outstanding requests for tracing of 874 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I asked you about the 874, and you gave me a whole lecture to confirm that number. And how many did you say there were missing persons in total until 1994 or as of 1994?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1.076 at the time I made my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many of these are Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sixty-four, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, let it stand. Let's assume it's correct. So if you take 64 Serbs, it's 1.012 Croats and a few others, a few Czechs, Ukrainians perhaps. It doesn't matter. But when you add this number of 64 to 874, it's 938 missing Serbs, according to your official records. Now, you are aware that according to official statistics, such as the census of 1991, let's put aside the fact that I have grave doubts about the validity of that 1991 census, there were about four and a half million Croats living in Croatia? Do you know how many?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, as far as I know, according to the census, I think there were less than four million people of Croatian nationality, but I really have reservations about this. This is not my area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Never mind. Even I don't know everything by heart. Around four million. And how many Serbs, according to official statistics, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, take it with a grain of salt, but I suppose that it's 500.000 to 600.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to official statistics, it's 580.000. I usually round it off. So there were seven to eight times more Croats than Serbs in the area of Croatia. We'll ignore the category of Yugoslavs, which was a form of Serb mimicry or a way to express mixed marriages. But isn't it striking that if there were seven to eight times more Croats in Croatia than Serbs, and if from this figure, 1.012, we deduct the Croats who went missing in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we deduct the members of these ethnic minorities, according to your official records an equal number of Croats as Serbs are still missing. Isn't that striking? Shouldn't that be proportionate to the population numbers? Try to answer it with a "yes" or "no" so we can move on.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is such a complex question that I can't answer it with a "yes" or "no." It's impossible. I'd like to emphasise two things here. First, the data we are talking about reflect the current situation, and the number of missing persons of Serb and Croat ethnicity is much higher than the figures we presented. In fact, it was much higher than the figures we presented, because such a large number of cases have been solved. Just let me finish. I find it very important to say the next thing concerning the comparison and the proportions between various categories of population, compared to the 1991 census. Statistically, such a comparison would not be justified. It would not be justified. But what would be justified would be to take into account the number and ethnic composition in areas that were affected by the war, not the territory of the Republic of Croatia as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that's something else. I fully understand you. However, if the number of missing Croats was far higher than you managed to solve those cases, the number of missing Croats then corresponded to the number of Serbs reported, and many Serbian families didn't want to report that their family members were missing, well, could that mean that you were far more expeditious and diligent when it came to locating missing Croats than when it came to locating missing Serbs, or is something else at stake?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let's -- before you answer the question just put by Mr. Seselj, I'd like to clear up one thing with you, because I think you started out by saying that the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons only registered Croatian nationals that had gone missing; and now it seems that apparently Serbian missing persons were also registered. So I just want to be sure whether the authorities of Croatia took upon themselves not only to register missing Croats, but also registering persons of other ethnicities, like Hungarians, or Serbs, or Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons kept records of all citizens of the Republic of Croatia, regardless of their ethnicity. So that included Croats, Serbs, Hungarians, all the citizens of the Republic of Croatia who had gone missing in the course of the war. Records were kept regardless of their nationality. Records were kept on the basis of the same criteria. If I can now answer Mr. Seselj's question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when you refer to the Republic of Croatia, are you talking about the republic that was part of the federal Yugoslav state or are you referring about the current republic and its current borders?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or is it the same? It doesn't matter what she has in mind, since the borders are identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, things are quite clear for me, but I believe that there may remain some level of doubt. You talked about the way that people were registered as missing persons, and you said that all Croatian nationals were registered, without any distinction being made in terms of their ethnicity. In other words, the thousand Serbs mentioned by Mr. Seselj who went missing, these Serbs were Croatian nationals, they were Serbs living in Croatia and nationals of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Yes, that's what I thought. In order to try and save time, it appears, out of all the questions put to you by the Defence, that as of today we have roughly the same number of Croats missing as Serbs, so we would roughly be talking about the same figure, 1.000 Serbs, 1.000 Croats; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's quite possible at this point in time -- or, rather, it's quite possible right now that there are more missing Croats, that the difference in the numbers of Serbs and Croats missing is not that great right now. However, for the sake of being objective and to give you a full picture of the situation, I would like to point out that the number of individuals who were registered as missing in the Republic of Croatia, well, there were far more of them who were Croatian nationality than there were of Serbian nationality. But at this point in time, as you said, these figures are very similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you now answer the question Mr. Seselj put to you initially?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj said that the families of missing Serbs didn't want to report the fact that family members of theirs had gone missing to the Croatian authorities. They didn't have to do so. They didn't have to report the fact to the Croatian authorities, if they didn't want to. But in such cases, the families would submit requests to locate missing individuals to the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And all these requests to locate them were entered into our records. So even those families that did not contact the Croatian authorities, if the missing family members were the responsibility of the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons, well, this administration would have them on their records. It's important. One has to understand that these records were complete, they were full. In addition to the International Committee of the Red Cross, the families --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with my question. You're wasting my time. I wouldn't mind if you were wasting the Judges' time or the Prosecution's time, but you're wasting my time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll move on to the second part of your question, because it was a conclusion. As far as your question is concerned, well, I can tell you that last year and the year before that year, the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons has completed the process of locating an identical number of individuals of Croatian nationality and individuals of Serbian nationality. However, until the time that we had information on missing individuals of Serbian nationality, until that time, until we had good information that would help us to find them, we couldn't solve the cases. Since information has been obtained, since exhumations have been carried out and body remains have been identified, well, since that time the number of solved cases with regard to missing Croats is about identical to the number of solved cases for missing Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, in the course of the proofing, you said that your access to the archives within your ministry wasn't complete, wasn't full, it wasn't unlimited. There's a part of the archives that contains some very sensitive information that you don't have access to; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had almost unlimited access to the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But not unlimited access?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even have to have totally unlimited access to the archives. I have access to the part of the archives that's important for me, as the head of the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Tell me, what is it that is so sensitive, so confidential, that prevents you, as a high-ranking civil servant, from having access to such information, and Ivan Grujic, the Colonel Ivan Grujic, has access to that? He's now been promoted to the rank of brigadier general; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I have said, my access to the archives is mostly unlimited.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please answer my question. What kind of material is so sensitive that you don't have access to it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Witness, do not beat about the bush, please. Apparently, during the proofing session with the Prosecutor, you told him that you were not able to have access to some sensitive archives. Mr. Seselj took note of that. He's putting a question to you about this, and it's very straightforward. Were you allowed to have access to all of the archives, or is it the case that you were not able to have access to some archives that may have been off limits because they were classified and secret archives? Could you please very candidly about this? You took the oath. You said that you were going to tell the truth and nothing but the truth. It's very important for us to know whether you had access to everything or only to part of the archives.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have access to the majority of documents contained in the archives. I don't have access to some documents. But it's not necessary for me to have access to such documents, given the work I do. But since I don't have access to those documents, I don't know really know what the contents of those documents are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me take a very simple case. As part of your work, let's assume you want to have access to documents related to the army. Are you entitled to go to the Croatian Ministry of Defence and have a look into their archives? This is a very specific question I'm asking you. What do you have to answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not go to the Ministry of Defence to familiarise myself with my -- with their archives, but there can be an official request that can have a certain level of confidentiality, in which I can explain the reasons for which I need access to some parts of the archives. And in such request, I can ask them to provide me with the relevant documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me take a very specific example. Let's assume that a Serb family in Belgrade gets in touch with the relevant administration, telling them, "We have a relative who disappeared in Croatia. He was detained in a camp run by the military." You said that this would go through the ICRC and that you would then be notified. So you are notified of this particular case. You are notified of the fact that this individual was detained in a military camp. What do you do in such a case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I submit a request to the relevant ministry for access with regard to the case in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since you say that you don't know anything about the contents of the sensitive part of the archives that you don't have access to, well, since that's what you say, I will now provide you with information; and then tell me what you think about it. The sensitive and confidential part of the archives, to which only Colonel Ivan Grujic has access, contains information on the exhumation of Serbs who were killed and who were located in 135 graves; and it also contains information on how one artificially reduced the number of victims in Pakracka Poljana and Malino Selo, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, for the following reason. The witness stated that since she did not have access to these documents, obviously she has no idea what they are; so I do not quite see how she could answer such a speculative question. And, furthermore, we do not know how Mr. Seselj would be, himself, aware of the nature of these documents. This is a very speculative question, and we have nothing telling us that these documents are the ones described by Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've interrupted the accused as he was putting his question to the witness. Let's wait for him to finish his question to decide whether it's a speculative question or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this isn't an ordinary witness who knows or doesn't know certain things. This is an expert who has to know everything. Not only does she have to know things that Mr. Dutertre doesn't know, but also things that I don't know. One can ask this expert for her expert opinion. This isn't a witness that speculates. It's a witness that can reflect and think, and she thinks in a far better manner than Mr. Dutertre. I'm quite happy about the way she thinks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please refrain from making personal attacks against this or that person, but put your question to the witness. Your question may be relevant, but we need to know what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm just providing you with a few examples out of the 135 graves in Pakracka Poljana and Malino Selo, which is in Western Slavonia, from October 1991 up until March 1992. Over 300 Serb civilians were killed, and your ministry has reduced this number 15-fold, and secret information on how many bodies were actually found is in the hands of Ivan Grujic and no one else. So the traces are lost of these others. And for another example, when it comes to the exhumation of Serbs, Serbian civilians who were shot in the Medak Pocket in 1986, and then we have Gospic, where over 200 Serbs -- almost 200 Serbs were killed. The figure is slightly lower. And you officially say that only 11 Serbian bodies were exhumed there. We're talking about Gospic now. That was in October 1991, roughly speaking. That's when they were killed. And then we have cases in many other places. One striking example is that many Serbian civilians were killed in Osijek, and Ivan Grujic was the local head of the State Security Service. That's what it was called at the time. First it was State Security and then the name was changed. The bodies of Serbs, in September and December 1991, of Serbs who were killed in Sarvas and Paulin Dvor, near Osijek. Osijek, Your Honours, is on the eastern edges, the estuary of the Drava and Danube. The bodies of Serbs killed in Paulin Dvor and Sarvas were found on Velebit in a place called Rizvanusa. Are you familiar with this, with the fact that the bodies of Serbs killed in Osijek were found on Velebit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I thought that Mr. Seselj was testifying. I was expecting a question, but he has finally put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Seselj has put a question to you. Please provide an answer, because we're dealing here with the very heart of the matter. The case of Mr. Seselj is that in your report, you give a number of Serbs that were killed, and he's given us a series of examples to illustrate the fact that according to him, many more Serbs were killed. What do you have to answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my report, there is information on all individuals who were exhumed and identified, individuals who were also of Serbian origin. I'm familiar with the exhumation on Rizvanusa. It's in my report as well. And victims from Paulin Dvor were found there, 17 of them. The institution I work in carried out the exhumation of the remains in Rizvanusa and identified the remains using the DNA method of analysis, and this institution organised the funeral of all those remains in accordance with their families' wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. I appreciate what you did, but Osijek is at the estuary of the river of Drava and Dunav; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And Rizvanusa is on Velebit, to the west of Lika, in the western part of Lika; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the distance, as the crow flies, is -- well, what would it be, about 400 kilometres, perhaps more?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about 400 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: About 400 kilometres. So someone from Osijek or Paulin Dvor and Sarvas near Osijek transported the Serbian bodies to conceal them on Velebit, which is very difficult to have access to; and the bodies were found. But the bodies of about 200 Serbs killed near Gospic still haven't been found; is that correct? The bodies of the Serbs killed in Osijek were found when this suited the regime for political reasons, because they wanted to deal with Branimir Glavas, who they didn't favour for political reasons, although he was one of the main persons responsible for those eliminations. But the bodies of the victims of military personnel who were in support of the regime haven't been found. So that's why some victims have been found and in other cases the bones found were destroyed. Am I right in saying this?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a compound question. Could it be divided up into a number of other questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's a very long question, it's a very complex question, but let me summarise it. According to Mr. Seselj, the bodies of those were not following the political line of the regime are found, but the bodies of the others are not to be found. What do you have to answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, in the question put to me by Mr. Seselj, information on victims was mentioned, information on victims of Serbian ethnicity, and this isn't supported by the documents. I'm not denying that people of Serbian ethnicity were killed, but, however, in Gospic a grave was exhumed, a grave in which the remains of 18 bodies were found. In the Medak Pocket, another grave was exhumed and the remains of 11 individuals were found there. In Pakracka Poljana, Mr. Seselj, in 1995 a grave was exhumed in which the remains of 19 individuals were found. And this shows that the Croatian authorities, the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons, carried out exhumations wherever they established that there might be graves, and this was regardless of the ethnic origins of the bodies of the people in those graves. There was nothing done for political reasons when it comes to exhuming remains, body remains. These remains were exhumed as soon as information was obtained about the possibility that there might be mass or individual graves at certain sites, and this was the case in all cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you don't know what the secret part of the archives in your ministry contains, the part of the archives you don't have access to. That's why your answer can't be complete. Please, could you tell me how much more time I have at my disposal so that I can plan for my cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell you shortly. 17 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Your ministry also became involved in the ideological process of rehabilitating the Ustasha movement, and they became involved with identifying it with a movement in the course -- the parties and movement in the course of the Second World War. You did this by exhuming the remains of Ustashas who were killed in the Second World War, and you buried them -- or they were buried again with certain honours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My ministry wasn't responsible for exhumations that date back to the Second World War, exhumation of bodies killed in the Second World War. However, given a particular decision of the government of Croatia, we were made responsible for exhuming certain remains, in technical terms, in order to take permanent care of certain remains. The administration did this whenever the government of Croatia issued such decisions. And I'll repeat, this was done regardless of the ethnic origins of the victims concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Listen to me carefully now, please. The independent state of Croatia, together with the Pavelic Ustasha regime, which acted as Hitler's satellite, sent 10.000 Ustasha volunteers to the Eastern Front as part of the so-called Croatian Legion. The Croatian Legion was routed at Stalingrad and the majority of its members were killed there. 16 Ustasha from that Croatian Legion died or were killed with a group of Italian soldiers. One division, more or less, was at the Eastern Front, and as the Italian military authorities collected their victims or exchanged -- or did an exchange for them and transported their remains to Rome, as they did this, they also took with them the remains of 16 Ustasha and buried them at the Roman cemetery, Cimitero Del Verano. And you, Ms. Bilic, together with Ivan Grujic, in 2007, on the 20th of December, 2007, went to Rome to take possession of the remains of these 16 Croatian soldiers, the remains that were in small boxes, and you transported them to Croatia. Religious rites were also performed on this occasion; is that correct? I have a document to this effect. I'm constantly being asked for documents, and I got this from the internet; and I even have a photograph. Mr. Dutertre has been provided with a copy. Why doesn't he look for it on the internet himself?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what is the relevance of this question with respect to the case, as submitted to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could I explain what the relevance is? In Belgrade, in the center of town, at the new town cemetery, there's a special French military grave where several hundred French soldiers, who were killed in the First World War, were buried. There is also a Soviet military grave there, and Russian soldiers who were killed in the Second World War, Russian soldiers fighting for the liberation of Belgrade, they were buried there. This cemetery is very beautiful, if we can describe a cemetery in this way. No one ever had the idea of moving these French or Russian soldiers back to their homelands, because they were buried in Belgrade with dignity. Italy is a civilised country, and it has its own military grave. Cimitero Del Verano is a cemetery which has a nice military grave. 16 Croatian soldiers, Ustashas, were also buried there. They were killed at the Eastern Front. They happened to be with the Italian soldiers who were killed, and they were transported there together. And after so much time has passed, a government, which is very similar to the Ustasha government from the Second World War, in terms of its programme and ideology, has the idea of requesting that the remains of 16 Ustasha be moved back from Rome to Croatia. This tells us a lot about the character of the government, about the ideology of the ministry that Ms. Bilic currently works for.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see the relevance of this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Bilic, he says you went to Rome, so what do you answer to this? I mean, we are here dealing with the credibility of the witness, so what do you say to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see from my CV, in 2002 I was appointed member of the Joint Commission for the Implementation of the Contract between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Italy, related to the casualties of World War II; and it is precisely on that basis, as a member of the Joint Commission, that I, together with other members of that commission, was notified about the mortal remains of 16 citizens of the Republic of Croatia that the Republic of Italy brought to Italy from Russia; and it was Italy that suggested we take over these mortal remains because they were the remains of people originating from Croatia. So these were the conclusions of a joint commission established by an agreement between two states, two governments, those of Croatia and Italy, and it was the realisation of one of the conclusions of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. If you had already started to implement these conclusions, did you exhume Italian citizens who were killed in the area of Dalmatia towards the end of the war, when around 300.000 Italians were killed or executed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Madam Bilic, I have a follow-up question. It seems that contrary to what Mr. Seselj is stating, it is not Croatia who went to get the 16 mortal remains, but it is upon a request by Italy that you actually went there. The Italians initiated the transfer. Obviously, this is what you're saying on page 27, line 4. And you can this within the framework of an agreement between Italy and Croatia. It seems to me it was the Italians that said, "We have 16 bodies. Please come and get them." Is that the way it occurred, or is it Croatia who said, "We know that there are 16 Croat nationals buried in Rome, and we would like the mortal remains of these 16 people"? Who initiated the whole proceeding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The notification on the mortal remains of these 16 persons was received from the Italian side, and it was their proposal that the Republic of Croatia take over these mortal remains, which was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, contrary to what you are stating, obviously the witness is saying the opposite of what you're stating.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's her job to say the opposite of what I'm saying, Mr. President. And when she's not able to, she will go on spinning her yarn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we're not here to try Croatia or to try the ideology of Croatia and so forth. I really do not see the relevance of this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometimes, to be quite frank, Madam Lattanzi, I forget who is on trial here, because looking at all the witnesses who have been here, and the evidence led, it always seems to me that I'm the Prosecutor here and the representatives of the OTP are actually defending the interests of my Serbian opponents in the past civil wars. But let me use the few remaining minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know, Ms. Bilic, that between 1991 and 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is totally unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you that personally, I really hate the Prosecution attacking Defence or Defence attacking the Prosecution. We're here to try and find out what happened. We have a report which was drafted by an expert witness. This report is challenged by -- at least some of the aspects of this report are challenged by the Defence, and credibility of the author of the report is also challenged. And the Judges need to know whether the data included in the report is reliable. We need to know that in order to draw our conclusions. So I'm asking Mr. Seselj and the Prosecution to focus on what is in the indictment, and only on what is in the indictment. Continue, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, here come a few easier questions, so relax. Do you know that between 1991 and 1995, on several occasions there were negotiations between the representatives of the government of the Serbian Krajina and the government of the Republic of Croatia on mutual exchanges of the dead; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in that period between 1991 and 1995, there were negotiations that discussed, among other things, deliveries and hand-overs of mortal remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that only in one case, in 1994, the Croatian authorities turned over to the authorities of Serbian Krajina 70 Serbian civilians, that is, bodies of Serbian civilians who had been exhumed in the territory of Zagreb in 1994? Were you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you know that at these meetings, they also agreed about exchanging living civilians? For instance, the government of the Serbian Krajina would look through the lists and search for detainees in Croatian camps, and Croatian authorities would look for their own nationals detained by Serbian authorities? Do you know there have been such exchanges of civilians?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there had been negotiations on exchanges, and there were exchanges of persons held by one or the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you for this brief answer. Do you know that the competent commission of the Republic of Croatia, led by Ivan Grujic, participated also in exchanges between the warring sides in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Those were exchanges of prisoners, exchanges of bodies, and exchanges of detained civilians.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that, and the then Commission for Detainees and Missing Persons was involved in the exchanges of prisoners and takeovers of mortal remains when the persons involved were from the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But there have also been detained civilians who were actually treated as hostages. One side would detain a certain number of civilians from the other side, and the other side would detain the same number, and then they bargain about an exchange?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In exchanges of civilians in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I actually can't think of a single case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you do have information about exchanges of civilians between the Serbian Krajina and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know, for instance, in the prison in Knin, there were villages of Marinovici, there were indisputably civilians. I know of several such cases where civilians were held in prison and were exchanged, because they had been in prisons in Beli Manastir, Knin, Glina, a whole series of locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But civilians on the opposite side, that is, your side, had also been held in prisons or improvised prisons, camps. You did not open -- make an announcement in the newspapers for Serbian civilians to come up and then be exchanged for Croats held in Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very leading question, and I cannot answer it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But I'm entitled to leading questions, aren't I? You know that, do you? Why am I asking that? Because Berislav Pusic, for instance, is on trial here, who as representative of Herceg-Bosna participated in exchanges of prisoners, civilians, and detainees; whereas Colonel Ivan Grujic is not on trial anywhere for exchanges of civilians. That is against the law, because civilians cannot be taken as hostages, according to international law, and even Ivan Grujic was involved in taking civilians hostages and even exchanging them for the other side.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said in my earlier answers, people were exchanged when they had been held by one or the other side. Concerning the Republic of Croatia, I said very explicitly that I know not of a single case of exchanges of civilians with Bosnia and Herzegovina, where the then Commission and now Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons was involved. So these claims that Colonel Grujic had been involved in the taking of hostages and exchanging of civilians are not correct, are not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Colonel Grujic confirmed in the Milosevic trial, the Mrksic trial, and other trials, I believe, Martic included, that he had been involved in negotiating such exchanges; and I have information, for instance, that he had personally been in Livno for one round of such negotiations, and you don't know that?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you tell me approximately at what time this happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The transcript only mentions negotiations in Livno, but unfortunately even I don't know the date, because the Prosecution had to give me the transcript of the examination of Ivan Grujic. He had been planned as an expert witness here, but he was so badly compromised that they had to switch. That's why you were so hastily taken as his replacement. You know that, don't you? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Colonel Grujic having been supposed to testify, I think that's the question you should ask the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. But you were produced here with such haste, as Grujic's replacement, that you had to write your expert report in great haste, and from the last expert report of Ivan Grujic, you copied the entire passages. I took the trouble of actually reading them and comparing them both, and underlining the passages that were copied.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not prepare my report in haste. I had ample time. It is a fact that the text of Deputy Minister Grujic is largely identical to the text of the report that I sent to the OTP, which is both justified and expected, because the report describes the methodology of our work, the results, and the status of our records. If you take that into account, it would be very odd if the reports were different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Reports cannot differ significantly in figures and data. But if you take whole sentences and paragraphs, then that would be plagiarizing, because Grujic's report is his author work and yours is yours. But I found whole passages pasted from Grujic's report in your report. That's plagiarism. Is that punishable in Croatia? In Serbia, you could be sentenced to prison. If you copied somebody's intellectual product and published it, that is approximately the legal provision, you would be sentenced to up to one year imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Bilic, I'm not talking about plagiarism here, but when the OTP commissioned you to draft this expert report, I guess that you had asked for Mr. Grujic's report, and you drafted your own report using Mr. Grujic's report as a base. Is this what you did? Did you read Mr. Grujic's report beforehand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. I compiled my report based on the report of the deputy minister, Colonel Grujic, and all the passages that remain unchanged, that is, those that relate to organisational aspects, the collection of information on missing persons, exhumations and identification, all those passages that are identical have been mostly taken over, as such, and put in my report. There was no need to change them because, as I said, they describe our methodology of work. All the new questions that the Prosecution included and asked me to cover in my report are there. All the data has been updated and included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have two minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But in that case, Ivan Grujic is your co-author, at least, which gives me the right to cross-examine him as well as you. Here, I found one page of the transcript in the Mrksic trial where Colonel Grujic confirms. That's page 10312, where Colonel Grujic confirms he had participated in exchanges of civilians between Croatia and Serbian Krajina and between the warring sides in Bosnia. That is information that I wanted to put to you, but I have no further questions, Ms. Bilic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Mr. Dutertre, any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to be as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because we have a break at 10.00. It would be good to finish by 10.00, because we have another witness waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To come back to this report, Ms. Bilic, you were based yourself on an internal document drafted by Mr. Grujic in order to write your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And you base yourself on the same statistical data; right?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, the same records, the same statistics, the same forms, because it's all about the methodology of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You told us that you updated the data, and as far as the rest is concerned, some information was not updated, but it was information that didn't have to change, but you checked the veracity of this --

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: This information was actually exact and true?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That information was correct, was accurate, and they reflect the state of records in the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons and the work processes that the administration is engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us the distance between Velebit Mountains and Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 450, perhaps 500 kilometres. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Regarding the seven non-identified persons among the Ovcara victims, page 11832-11834 of today's transcript, you were asked some very speculative questions, so I'll do the same. So is it possible that the relatives of these people could live in Croatia and had not been -- had not heard about this information, collection campaign, or could it be that these people come from Croatia, but actually had no relatives, and that's why no one actually identified these seven bodies, because actually no one claimed them?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's also possible that they did not have any family members who would look for them, that entire families were dead, or perhaps they did not have enough relevant family members or next of kin that DNA analysis would be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Next item, and it was at page 11, line 14 and 15, in today's transcript. This proportion of ethnicity, proportion of ethnicity. Could you confirm that among the exhumed people for which the identity was established that 87 per cent of them were Croats? This was in document 7362 of the 65 ter list that we saw yesterday. 87 per cent.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. 87 percent of identified persons are of Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Now let's talk about the people who were still gone missing. I'm having a hard time tracking all this, but I'm sure Mr. Seselj won't blame me for this. We have document 761 in the first binder, the blue binder. Could you please take a look at this document. In this document, there is mention of the 1.076 people who are still gone missing. I repeat the number of the document, 7361 [Realtime transcript read in error, "761"] in the first binder, the blue binder. The "3" is still missing, 7361. So in this document, on the sixth page in the English version, we have the nationality of the people gone missing of these 1.076 people that have gone missing, and we can note that 87 are Croats. Do you confirm this figure, that there are only 64 Serbs among these people gone missing?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: The English transcript does not reflect what I heard in my headset in French. Could you please repeat your answer, Ms. Bilic?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that was correct. 87 per cent of missing persons are of Croat ethnicity, and among the missing persons there are 64 Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Now, quickly and in order to supplement the questions that we mentioned this morning on page 7 and 8, and yesterday, page 11834 of the transcript, so if a French family, a Serb family, an Italian family, inquires with the Administration of Missing Persons, saying, "This persons disappeared on the territory of Croatia between 1991 and 1995," could you tell us exactly what you would do after having obtained this inquiry from this family?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We will receive a tracing request if it's within the jurisdiction of the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons. And if it is not, in that case we would tell the family to approach the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: One last question. Yesterday, page 11842 to 11845 in the transcript, you were asked a question on the Serb detainees in Croatia, and we mentioned this again today. Your report has little information on the detainees held by Croat authorities during the conflict, but is it because this is -- this comes under the aegis of another ministry, for example the Ministry of Defence, and has its own information; and you're not in charge of collecting this information? Or is it a deliberate choice to have decided not to address this question in your report?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we can see from the decrees of the Republic of Croatia government, governing issues of detainees and missing persons, the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons is not in charge of keeping records of persons who were in the hands of the Republic of Croatia authorities. It's the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of Defence, not our ministry, that are in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have just completed your testimony. On my behalf and on behalf of my colleagues, I would like to thank you for having come to testify for the Prosecution in this case in relation to missing persons who are victims of the conflict of the former Yugoslavia. I wish you a safe trip home. The usher will now escort you out of the courtroom, and thus you'll be able to take your plane home. We're going to have a 20-minute break now. After that break, we'll have the following witness. With respect to the documents, Mr. Dutertre, the documents you offered into evidence, you've already listed them yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we have to add 65 ter document 7361.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will rule in writing about these documents. We'll have a 20-minute break, and we'll resume then with the following witness. The Prosecution will have one hour to examine the witness, and Mr. Seselj one hour to cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Please state your first name, last name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Katica Paulic, the 1st of April, 1956.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a profession, an occupation? If so, which one is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am now an employee in the company called Elektrocontact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you ever testified before a court about the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia, or is it the first time you're going to testify about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the first time today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please read the solemn declaration the usher is going to show to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me give you some explanation. You will answer questions put to you by Mr. Ferrara, whom you've probably met as part of preparation of your testimony. Mr. Ferrara will ask you questions and show you a number of documents. If necessary, the Judges will also put questions to you. Mr. Seselj, who is the accused in this case, will also put questions to you as part of the cross-examination. That's the way we are going to proceed. I'm not sure whether we'll be able to complete your testimony today. Barring any incidents, this should be possible, but we also may have to continue with your testimony tomorrow morning. I can't tell you anything at this stage. I'm trying not to waste any time at all, and I'm immediately going to give the floor to Mr. Ferrara. He has one hour to examine you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I want to point out that the witness has some health problems, so maybe it's possible that she will ask to break or something if she feels not well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I was not aware that you had health problems. If you feel unwell at any time, raise your hand and ask for the hearing to be adjourned. But it's up to you, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Ms. Paulic, when were you born, and how long did you live there?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 1st of April, 1956, and I lived there permanently up until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: In Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What's your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: I am a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Where do you currently live?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: I live in Zagreb, where I exchanged my house. That's where I exchanged a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What was your occupation and employment in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: I was involved in agricultural labour for a while, until we built a house, and then I opened up my own shop in my very own house. So I ran a shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What was the ethnic makeup of Hrtkovci in 19 -- until 1992?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: Up until 1992, well, briefly, I would put it like this: It was super. There was no stress. We got on well. We had lunch at each other's places. We celebrated Easter and Christmas, et cetera, together. Everything was excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So can you give us an estimate of the different ethnic group in Hrtkovci at that time?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: At the time, there were a lot of Croats, Hungarians. They had been there for a long time because the village is an old one. There were Hungarians and Germans. The Germans were expelled, the Hungarians stayed on. Serbs from Slavonia moved in. Bosnians and Dalmatians moved in. People from Lika moved in. They were all in the minority. Croats were the majority, and there were somewhat fewer Hungarians than there were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: You say that everything was excellent. When -- this relationship changed, and when?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When did this change?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: Well, the relationship started changing when the war broke out in Croatia. Shortly afterwards, after Vukovar, people from Slavonia started arriving, various strangers started arriving in the village. They acted in a disruptive manner in the village. They made everyone nervous. That's when things started.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When did you start hearing people talking about ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: Well, since I ran a shop, my neighbour who lived across the road, Slavko Mirazic, who was a calm boy, to tell you the truth; but he started spreading rumours according to which the Croats didn't know what was waiting for them, that there would be ethnic cleansing, and then he had a list of those who would be leaving. Those were the words used, and that's the first I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of this Slavko Mirazic?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: A Serb, a Serb. Both his father and mother were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did he belong to any political party?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: Yes. He would always boast that he belonged to Seselj parties, that he knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How do you know he belonged to this party? He told you?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: That's what he said, yes. He said that. He would come to my shop, and he used those very words.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: You say that as the war was spreading in Croatia, there was this -- the refugees start -- people from East Slavonia start to arrive in your village. How many refugees would you estimate arrived in Hrtkovci in 1992?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: Well, look, it's very difficult to give you a number, because this occurred on a daily basis. They would move around in groups. There would be four or five of them together, sometimes ten of them together, sometimes four of them in a group. It depended on the kind of groups they formed, but this was a daily and continual occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Were they organised in some way or they arrived on initiative -- their initiative?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: I believe that they were organised, because initially they moved around. Well, they were most interested in large houses, to start with. They weren't really interested in small houses. They were interested in large houses, and that's where they would go. That's what they would attack. I can provide you with a few examples. They'd come to me, and I also know the lady across the road, not exactly across the road; but to my right there was an old granny who lived there. Her son was in Germany, and naturally a new house was built. It was a new house full of everything, lots of tools. There was lots of furniture and other things in the house. The old lady died and the son remained in Germany. The son had to sell the house. He sold the house to a man and woman who also lived abroad, and they would come, well, occasionally. They'd spend a few days in the house. They returned to Hungary, a bit of the weekend remained. At the time the Serbs arrived, they moved into the house. They did that overnight. They opened the house up and they moved in. Someone reported this to the couple. They told them that people had moved into the house. They returned then. The lady reported the fact to the police there, and she wasn't able to achieve anything through this means. She came to my shop and she told me that she was looking for a few dresses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When did it happen, this event?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: Before Seselj arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When did Seselj arrive in Hrtkovci, just to have a clear idea?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: That was when these people were involved in the attacks. That's what I'm talking about. She literally asked me to let her go to the toilet, to let her use my toilet, because she couldn't enter her own house, and she didn't gain access to her house.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Were these Serb refugees viewing only houses or other people in Hrtkovci or businesses as well, like shops or factories?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I had my shop, my own shop. Naturally, Zdenko Barisic also had his own shop. He also worked in the local commune as a secretary in the local commune. The case was the same for him. The people who were called out, well, they were all in power. But people were interested in large houses. My uncle has a small, miniature house, so he wasn't affected. But we were, because we had big houses. When I say "a big house," I don't know what you consider to be a big house, but they were big houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you receive any visit from any of the refugees in your shop?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, many.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When, and what they told you?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: It was like this: When you enter the shop, there was a sort of storage space to the left. They would sometimes open it up and say, "Well, it's good, that could be ours." They said it's better to go there with a bag. They used a local word for "bag." They said, "It's better for you to go out like this than leave with a bag in your hand." Well, that, in effect, meant you should leave, you should go. I could go on about these people for an entire day, but I'll select a number of examples. There was someone called Jovo. He was tall, wore a beard, and he would bring these people in. And on one occasion, he appeared on his own. I remember that well. It's as if it happened yesterday. It was on a Sunday. I was working on my own. My employee had the day off. I was working there alone. There was a long queue. When I saw him, I was afraid, naturally. I served the customers, I don't know how. It doesn't even matter. When it was his turn, I mustered all my courage and briefly asked him, "How can I help you?" He was a customer, but I knew why he was there. He said he wasn't going to buy anything. He said the following: He said, "Madam, I admit that I'm bringing other people in here to exchange houses. You should leave your house. Well, I have a house in Zagreb, so it would be better for you to go to Zagreb. Zagreb is the capital," and so on and so forth. He said I should go to Zagreb. I then mustered all my courage, or the courage just appeared of its own accord, and then I told him quite clearly and loudly, "What kind of a man are you? Look at yourself. You have come here to expel me and to talk to me. Go and see my husband." My husband was in the center. "Go and see him," I told him, "and speak to him about this." And he really did go away, and he found my husband, and he told my husband, "Your wife is someone to be reckoned with. She expelled me." There were other incidents. On one occasion, my employee was working there. I'd gone to town to pay something in the bank, to pay some bills. My husband went away to collect some goods, because he was working with me at the time. The shop was doing well. The employee was also working. Then a group attacked the shop, another group attacked the door, the door that I used to enter my house. They wanted to come in. They swore a bit. We're talking about a married woman, and when I say they swore a bit, they cursed. This married woman, she wanted to defend herself. They told her, "What do you know?" Her younger son is in the ZNG. The ZNG didn't even exist there, how can a child who goes to the seventh class and is 14 years old be a member of the ZNG? She didn't allow this to happen. She quickly contacted her husband and told him to come. She said that there was some strangers there. That's what we called them. He appeared. They left, and they said they would be back, but they probably saw him and didn't return.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you -- did you receive any phone calls concerning the threats that --

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you describe? Can you describe?

utterances.speaker: KATICA PAULIC
utterances.text: I can, I can. Since I use the phone a lot because of the shop, well, it was early evening I left the receiver -- well, it might be difficult to describe this for you because you are not familiar with the Zagreb dialect and Serbian dialects; but I'll explain this for you. I'll quote this person. He said, "Look after your child, take care of your child. We'll come now." But in Serbia, they say, "Look after your child." "Dete" is the word used, not "dijete," "because we'll come now." Again, I mustered my courage and I said, "Come, come, just you come and we'll see." What else could I have said? But he threatened me -- this is an assumption of mine, not a conclusion; but I think he threatened to do something to my younger child, because he was in the seventh grade, and the older child was not staying at home. I told my husband about what had occurred. He reported it to the police, and the police said, "What can we do? You should disconnect the phone." He said, "I can't disconnect the phone.
